To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
TGFB1 and TGFB1 signaling are modified in the spinal cord, muscle and blood of ALS mice and humans.
TGFB1 signaling is altered at presymptomatic and symptomatic stage in the spinal cord, and at presymptopathic stage selectively in the skeletal muscle of male ALS mice.
TGFB1 signaling is altered both in the spinal cord of amyotrophic lateralsclerosis (ALS) mice and in the muscle of both male and female ALS patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of the transforming growth factor beta (TGF-beta) signaling pathway in the pathogenesis and progression of amyotrophic laterial sclerosis (ALS).
gender differences in the expression of TGFbeta and its signaling molecules in the skeletal muscle and the spinal cord of ALS patients.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

TGFB1 is increased in the skeletal muscle at presymptomatic and symptomatic stages in ALS, whereas it is reduced in the spinal cord at the presymptomatic stages and augmented at the symptomatic stages.
TGFB1 signaling is altered both in the spinal cord (Tgfbr2 and Smad2) and in skeletal muscle (Tgfb1, Smad3, Pax7, Collagen, and Fibronectomy) in ALS patients and in mice.

the expression of TGFB1 signaling molecules is altered in the muscle of male ALS mice and in the muscle of sporadic ALS patients, suggesting that TGFB1 signaling may be a therapeutic target for ALS, particularly in male patients.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the gender-related differences in the TGFB1 pathway in the spinal cord, and the gender and disease stage-related differences in the muscle, are likely to contribute to the pathogenesis of ALS.
TGFB1 is a potential therapeutic target for ALS and that the gender differences observed may be related to the differential expression of Smad2 and/or Smad3.
TGFB1 signaling is altered both in the spinal cord, and in the skeletal muscle of male ALS mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TGFβ signaling is altered in both the spinal cord and the skeletal muscle of ALS patients and that gender differences may play a role in the pathophysiology of ALS.
TGFB1 and SMAD signaling are modified in the spinal cord of ALS mice and patients and in the skeletal muscle of ALS patients, and that these changes may represent a novel therapeutic target.
TGFβ1 is increased in the muscle of both ALS mice and patients, suggesting that this cytokine may be a therapeutic target in ALS.
